# Prompting FLUX video

Models: FLUX.3. A good prompt runs about 1200 characters.

Name each reference where the prompt uses it as `@{ref:<ref>}`, with the exact ref you pass; Sceneform swaps in the model's own token, so wherever this guide names a token (`@Image1`, `Figure 1`), write the mention instead.

FLUX.3 video takes anything from one line to a directed brief. Black Forest Labs' rule is to direct a scene, not list objects: say what happens, how the subject moves, what the camera does, and what it sounds like, in concrete nouns and verbs the camera can see.

**Length.** A short prompt hands framing, motion and mood to the model; a longer one gives control. Add camera, motion and atmosphere only where they change the result. Over-stuffing makes the motion less coherent.

**One shot.** The default form is one flowing sentence or two: the shot, the subject and its action, the place, then the supporting visual and motion details. "A red fox stalks across a wide snowfield at dawn, low winter light, a dark treeline fading into mist behind it. It slows, crouches, then leaps high and pounces into the fresh snow. Telephoto lens, shallow depth of field, locked-off camera panning gently to follow. Muffled paw steps and a soft breeze."

**Camera.** One framing term, one movement term, one clear action. "Low tracking shot" reads; "low aerial handheld orbit push-in" does not. Terms from Black Forest Labs' list: extreme close-up, close-up, wide shot, Dutch angle; dolly in, push through, tracking shot, Steadicam follow, handheld, crane, orbit, tilt up, slow pan, whip pan, dolly zoom, rack focus. Pair a term with what it shows: "tilt up from muddy boots to a storm-lit face".

**Timed beats.** Only when the action has to land at a moment, write a short timeline, two or three beats for a five-second clip, each one achievable:

0.0-1.5s: locked wide of a still harbor at dawn, boats motionless on glassy water.
1.5-3.0s: a slow push-in begins as gulls lift off the water.

**Several shots in one clip.** Only when the request carries distinct shots, label them and mark each cut: "SHOT ONE: wide aerial of a desert highway at dawn. HARD CUT. SHOT TWO: interior close-up, the driver's hands drumming the wheel." Open with one line that states the whole arc, keep the subject description word for word identical in every shot, and say whether one music bed runs across all of them.

**Sound.** Audio renders with the picture, so write it in. Footsteps, impacts, rain, engines and crowd motion give it the clearest material. Name each sound by its source and tie effects to visible actions: "the mug clicks against the saucer when he sets it down", not "moody ambience". Keep to the one or two layers the scene needs. Name the sound you want rather than asking for silence: "quiet room tone" can collapse into static.

**Speech.** Quote the exact words and say who delivers them: She looks toward the passenger and says, "The 6:10 is delayed again." For an off-screen line, call it a voiceover or narration, or the words may be drawn into the frame as text. Direct the voice with a few concrete anchors: age and accent when they matter, the recording ("close and dry", "over a phone speaker"), and the delivery ("lightly amused, talking to one friend"). Keep lines short enough to say in the clip, name the language beside each line, and close any prompt with speech with "No on-screen text, no subtitles."

**With a start frame.** The image is the exact first frame, so the prompt carries only the motion and the camera: "push forward through the trees". With a start and an end frame, describe the one transition that carries the first into the second.

**Extend.** Only FLUX.3 Extend continues a source clip. The source clip sets the subjects, motion and look. Describe how the same shot keeps unfolding without a cut, continuing the current action: "A herd of elephants walks steadily toward the camera across a dry savanna, the animals growing larger in frame as the sun sinks lower behind them."

**Text in the frame.** Quote the words and describe where and how they appear: "a bold kinetic title card, the word "FLUX" assembling from light streaks on a dark stage".

**Avoid.** Vague adjectives where a visible detail would do the work. Several camera moves in one sentence. A long script, several speakers and several visual beats forced into a short clip. Overlapping dialogue.
